web.markdown:
# FAQ

## Transport

### QWhere is the starting point of the Alpine Route?

A

Tateyama Station (Toyama Prefecture, west side) and Ogizawa (Nagano Prefecture, east side).

### QWhat time are the first and last departures?

A

It varies depending on the season. Please see the [timetable](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/timetable/).

### QDo I need a reservation to ride?

A

Only the Tateyama Cable Car departing Tateyama Station, and the Kanden Tunnel Electric Bus departing Ogizawa, require a designated boarding time. You can reserve a departure time when purchasing web tickets, but for other advance tickets and same-day tickets, boarding times must be reserved at the station’s ticket window. Reservations are not required at other stations, so please check the timetable and head to the boarding gate accordingly.

### QCan I get on and off the Tateyama Highland Bus along its route?

A

You can get off at Midagahara and Tengudaira. However, because all passengers are required to be seated, reservations are required to re-board the bus.

If you get off at Midagahara, please make your re-boarding reservation at Midagahara Station.

If you get off at Tengudaira, please make your reservation at Tengudaira Mountain Lodge.

### QCan I get off at each station for sightseeing?

A

You can enjoy sightseeing and walking around at each station during your transfers. Please check the timetable and ensure that you do not miss your transfer.

### QAre parking lots available if I come by car?

A

There are [parking lots](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/parking/) at Tateyama Station (Toyama side) and at Ogizawa (Nagano side). Cars are not permitted on the Alpine Route (between Tateyama Station & Ogizawa), so if you are passing through, please use the car [forwarding service](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/getting-here/#VehicleTransferService).

## Tickets

### QWhere can I buy tickets?

A

1\. Purchase your web ticket in advance through the [official website](https://tateyama-kurobe-webservice.jp/AlpenTour/html/VW001W0010.html). (You must collect your ticket from the ticket machine before boarding.)

2\. Purchase tickets in advance through a travel agency. Tickets must be exchanged, and departure times reserved, on the day of travel.

3\. Purchase [same-day tickets](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/same-day-tickets/) at Alpine Route stations. (Tickets cannot be purchased the day before travel.)

### QCan I purchase same-day tickets even if web tickets are sold out?

A

Yes. Even when web tickets are sold out, same day tickets will remain available, but your desired departure time may be fully booked and additional waits may be required.

### QWhat time does the ticket sales counter open?

A

At Tateyama Station it opens 20 min before the first departure time, and at Ogizawa Station it is 40 min in advance.

The Alpine Route ticket window at Dentetsu Toyama Station usually opens at 7:30 but may open as early as 5:00 on certain days. If you are departing Dentetsu Toyama Station early in the morning, please purchase only your train ticket at first, and then purchase tickets for the additional routes on your journey upon arrival at Tateyama Station.

### QCan I purchase or exchange tickets at the station ticket window on the day before travel?

A

Ticket purchases and exchanges cannot be made the day before travel. Please come to the ticket window on the day that you will use the tickets.

### QCan I pay by credit card?

A

Cards can be used at Dentetsu Toyama, Tateyama, Bijodaira, Midagahara, Murodo, Daikanbo, Kurobedaira, Kurobeko, Kurobe Dam, and Ogizawa stations.

### QDo I need to buy a ticket for each section of the route?

A

Both one-way and round-trip tickets are available and cover all sections to your destination. However, depending on the station, tickets for some sections may not be available.

### QI am staying at a hotel on the Alpine Route. Can I use my ticket the next day?

A

Your ticket is valid for 5 days from the first day of use, for both one-way & round-trip travel.

## Sightseeing

### QHow long does it take to see the sights along the Alpine Route?

A

The journey from Tateyama Station to Ogizawa usually takes 6-8 hours, including transfers and sightseeing time. It is expected to be particularly busy during the snow wall season and on Japanese holidays, so please allow yourself plenty of time.

See suggested [model course](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/how-to-enjoy/sightseeing/from-toyama/) for details."

### QWhen does the sightseeing water release take place at Kurobe Dam?

A

Water sprays continuously throughout the day from June 26 to October 15. The water release may be canceled due to weather conditions.

### QCan I fly unmanned aerial vehicles (drones)?

A

The use of drones is not permitted.

### QHow do I get to Mikurigaike pond?

A

Go up the stairs at Murodo Station and turn left from the rooftop. You will reach the photo spot in about 15 min.

### QHow do I get to the snow wall?

A

After getting off the bus at Murodo Station, the highest point of the snow wall is a 15 min walk from the designated entrance. Snow wall touring can be enjoyed from mid-April till late June.

### QWhen can I see the fall leaves?

A

The elevation changes by 2,000 m across the Alpine Route, so the best viewing time varies from spot to spot. Mid-September till early November is considered the best viewing time.

### QAre there any locations where I can enjoy hiking?

A

There are a variety of hiking trails in Murodo, as well as some in Midagahara and Bijodaira.

### QWhat are the temperatures and recommended clothing for each season?

A

At the highest point on the Alpine Route (Murodo 2,450 m), temperatures are about 15℃ (60℉) lower than at sea level. Please refer to the followings for temperatures (at Murodo elevation 2,450 m) and clothing recommendations

### QWhat are the best places to stay, on and around the Alpine Route?

A

Toyama City, around Tateyama Station, Matsumoto City, Omachi City, Omachi Onsenkyo(Omachi Hot Springs) and Nagano City are good places to stay before or after visiting.

On the Alpine Route itself, accommodation is available at Midagahara Hotel, Mikurigaike Onsen (hot springs), Murodo Mountain Lodge, and Tengudaira Mountain Lodge.

## Facilities

### QIs there a baggage forwarding service?

A

A baggage forwarding service is available that allows you to collect your luggage on the same day. [See details here](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/baggage/).

### QIs there a car forwarding service?

A

There is a car forwarding service between Tateyama Station & Ogizawa. [See details here](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/getting-here/#VehicleTransferService).

### QAre there any coin lockers?

A

Coin lockers are available at Tateyama, Bijodaira, Midagahara, Murodo, Kurobe Dam, and Ogizawa stations.

### QAre there any locations where drinking water is available?

A

Water is available at Tateyama, Murodo, Kurobedaira, and Kurobe Dam stations. Please ask staff for more information at each location.

### QAre there any elevators?

A

Elevators are only in operation at Ogizawa Station and Tateyama Nature Conservation Center (Murodo). Please speak to a member of staff if you require assistance.

### QAre wheelchairs available?

A

Wheelchairs are placed at each station for backup and emergency use. However, it is not possible to use one chair continuously across the Alpine Route.

### QAre baby carriages available to rent?

A

We do not provide baby carriage rentals. Furthermore, we recommend using compact carriages as there are many stairs and transfers.

### QIs smoking permitted?

A

Smoking is permitted only within the designated smoking area at each station.

### QWill I be able to use my mobile phone and Wi-fi?

A

Mobile phones get reception at most stations.

Wi-fi is available, free of charge, at Tateyama, Bijodaira, Murodo, Daikanbo, Kurobedaira, and Kurobeko stations. E-mail authentication is required, so it’s convenient to register in advance.

### QAre there any ATMs?

A

There are no ATMs along the length of the Alpine Route.

The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route's a fun day trip in Japan. It's a mountain adventure on trains, buses, cable cars and ropeways, where you can see up to 20 foot snow walls, even in June!

✨ Get my 300 page Japan guide book: [https://cakeswithfaces.co.uk/product/...](https://www.youtube.com/redirect?event=video_description&redir_token=QUZZTVljR0U2ZVZ0Zi0tRWtoSk91Vlk0MEJOcXxBTl9pYzRmTHlCTXZud2VMaFhYbGd4bXFNRjhmeGg5OEt6cHE3ZmRRVGF2VUtnYzlubmh0b1ZxR09fSGRBblRfX28yQUQ2VEE4allXZWJUQmVmbU4tbjBwMVQ4b0dyMVpfYUF4&q=https%3A%2F%2Fcakeswithfaces.co.uk%2Fproduct%2Fjapan-travel-guide-book%2F&v=1lD9_CbtuvE)

An off the beaten track day trip in Japan! You can do the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route in either direction. We started in Toyama and ended in Nagano, then took the shinkansen back to Tokyo. It's also easy to reach from Kanazawa. The video includes how to get tickets, where to pick up your tickets and all the things I wanted to know before I went, with lots of tips! I went at the start of June, and the snow walls (yuki otani) were still 13m high. They were so impressive! It's snowy in Murodo until the end of June, and the mountain route's open from mid April until the end of November. You use multiple forms of transport including a ropeway, tunnel bus, cable-car and trains, to travel through the mountains on a day trip. The highlights are Murodo (the highest point, with the snow walls), the views at Daikanbo, Bijodaira and the Kurobe Dam, which is the tallest dam in Japan. It's also stunning in fall with the autumn colours. Along the way you also see Shomyo Falls. It's a very easy day trip with no driving and no hiking, but you still have the freedom to spend as long as you want in each place.

web.markdown:
![](https://www.japan-guide.com/thumb/XYZeXYZe7550_1680.jpg)

The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route (立山黒部アルペンルート, Tateyama Kurobe Alpen Route) is a unique and spectacular route through the [Northern Japan Alps](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e6043.html) which is traversed by various means of transportation including cablecars, electric buses and a ropeway. Completed in 1971, the route connects [Toyama City](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7500.html) in [Toyama Prefecture](https://www.japan-guide.com/list/e1219.html) with Omachi Town in [Nagano Prefecture](https://www.japan-guide.com/list/e1216.html). The section between Tateyama Station and Ogizawa is closed to private vehicles.

The route is **open from April 15 to November 30** and inaccessible during the winter.

![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g25/7550_2504.gif)

The main attraction of the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route is the magnificent scenery of the Tateyama Mountain Range, part of the [Chubu Sangaku National Park](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e6043.html). Visitors can enjoy varying vistas during different seasons of the year. In spring, accumulated snow, especially around the upper sections of [Midagahara](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7555.html) and [Murodo](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7553.html), form a majestic **snow corridor** whose [snow walls](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7550.html#snow) reach up to 20 meters high. A section of the snow corridor around Murodo is open to pedestrians from April 15 to June 25.

Summer and autumn attract visitors with beautiful landscapes, alpine flowers (especially June to August) and [autumn leaves](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2014.html). The fall colors typically reach their best around Murodo and Daikanbo from late September to early October, and they gradually descend the mountain slopes, arriving at the lower elevations around late October to early November.

![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g21/7550_01.jpg)

Autumn colors can be seen along the Alpine Route from late September into early November

The highest point along the route, [Murodo](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7553.html) offers a variety of [hiking](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2427.html) trails that cater both to serious hikers and to those looking for a leisurely walk. Other highlights along the route are the single-span Tateyama Ropeway that provides great panoramic bird's eye views of the surrounding mountain scenery, and the 186 meter tall [Kurobe Dam](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7554.html) which is especially spectacular when it discharges water between late June and mid October.

From mid June through September temperatures along the Alpen Route are mild, and it rarely gets too hot either. From April to early May and from mid October through November, temperatures are cool and it might get chilly on windy days. Just one layer of clothing is enough for summer, while an additional sweater or jumper is recommended for spring and autumn. Good walking shoes are advised if you plan on hiking beyond the easy walking trails in the vicinity of the respective stations along the route. [Accommodation](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2025.html) in the form of hotels, mountain huts and camp grounds is available along the route, especially around Murodo.

![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g21/7550_02.jpg)

Tateyama Ropeway

The following is a list of transportation and attractions along the Alpine Route, in order from west to east:

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_05.jpg)











Toyama Chiho Railway




Running through rural [Toyama Prefecture](https://www.japan-guide.com/list/e1219.html), this train gets you from Dentetsu Toyama Station (next to JR Toyama Station) in central [Toyama City](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7500.html) to Tateyama Station in about one hour. It runs around the year. The one way fare is 1420 yen.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_06.jpg)











Tateyama Cablecar




The Tateyama Cablecar ascends from Tateyama Station to Bijodaira Station in seven minutes. The one way fare is 1090 yen. Tickets need to be purchased for a specific departure time in the direction of Murodo and can be reserved in advance by purchasing a [Web Ticket](https://tateyama-kurobe-webservice.jp/AlpenTour/html/VW001W0010.html).

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_07.jpg)











Highland Bus




This bus requires roughly 50 minutes for the journey between Bijodaira Station and Murodo. The one way fare is 3000 yen. There are a few stops along the way, including the [Midagahara Wetlands](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7555.html). During spring, the bus runs along the [Tateyama Snow Corridor](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7550.html#snow).

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_08.jpg)









[Tateyama Snow Corridor](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7553.html)


From April to May, the road from Bijodaira to Murodo runs between up to 20 meter high snow walls. The snow corridor is most spectacular around [Murodo](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7553.html), where an approximately one kilometer passage is open to pedestrians from around mid April to mid June.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_09.jpg)









[Murodo](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7553.html)

[Murodo](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7553.html) offers fantastic views of the Tateyama Mountain Range. In summer and autumn, hiking trails lead to the surrounding peaks and to the nearby Jigokudani "Hell Valley". Volcanic activity can be observed at the valley, although the trails in the area can get closed due to high concentrations of volcanic gases.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g25/7550_tateyama_bus.jpg)











Tateyama Tunnel Electric Bus




Electric buses transport travelers through the tunnel between Murodo and Daikanbo. The one way journey takes 10 minutes and costs 2200 yen.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_11.jpg)











Daikanbo




This is the transfer station between the Tateyama Tunnel Electric Bus and the Tateyama Ropeway. The small station has an observation deck with great views of the mountains.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_12.jpg)











Tateyama Ropeway




This 1.7 kilometer long ropeway operates without any support towers between the lower and upper stations, making it Japan's longest one-span ropeway. The one way trip takes seven minutes and costs 1700 yen. Due to the ropeway's relatively small capacity, it can be a bottleneck on busy days.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_13.jpg)











Kurobedaira




Kurobedaira is the transfer station between the Tateyama Ropeway and Kurobe Cablecar. The station offers a restaurant, souvenir shop and beautiful views of the surrounding mountains.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_14.jpg)











Kurobe Cablecar




This cablecar runs entirely inside a tunnel, which is a rarity among cablecars. The one way journey between Kurobedaira and Kurobeko Station (next to Kurobe Dam) takes five minutes and costs 1150 yen.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_15.jpg)









[Kurobe Dam](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7554.html)

[Kurobe Dam](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e7554.html), with a height of 186 meters, is Japan's tallest dam. From late June to mid October, up to 15 tons of water per second are spectacularly discharged through the dam.

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g19/7550_ebus.jpg)











Kanden Tunnel Bus




Electric buses transport travelers through the tunnel between Kurobe Dam and Ogizawa. The one way journey takes 15 minutes and costs 1800 yen. Tickets need to be purchased for a specific departure time in the direction of Murodo and can be reserved in advance by purchasing a [Web Ticket](https://tateyama-kurobe-webservice.jp/AlpenTour/html/VW001W0010.html).

- ![](https://www.japan-guide.com/g3/7550_17.jpg)











Ogizawa-Omachi Bus




A regular bus service connects Ogizawa with JR Shinano-Omachi Station via Omachi Onsen. The one way trip takes 40 minutes and costs 1650 yen. There are also direct buses between Ogizawa and [Nagano City](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e6000.html) (105 minutes, 4300 yen one way).

web.markdown:
Opening page [Skip to main content](https://valunavi.com/post/tateyama-kurobe-summer-route-murodo-dam-guide/#main) ![Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route in Summer: Murodo, Dam and Timing](https://valnavi-cms-api-production.tsechun1227.workers.dev/media/variants/b1461733-f9d9-4705-a8df-2976e70c116d/a96e72403708194d5fe31fb387ed67de2dc876b84055ba9c1788b35e5bd5a049/960w-028748d942eee74099b03903c307586e6e4ad1c72e4438e57b9577493e6afb10.webp) ![Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route in Summer: Murodo, Dam and Timing](https://valunavi.com/api/media/939943df-f9b4-43db-b561-611323e79d77/original) **Cross the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route in one direction when it can replace a normal Toyama–Nagano transfer; do a return trip only when Murodo or Kurobe Dam is the real destination.** The route is not one train. It is a sequence of trains, cable cars, buses, ropeways and walking sections between Tateyama Station in Toyama and Ogizawa in Nagano. The official 2026 same-day guidance budgets roughly 7–8 hours for a Dentetsu Toyama → Ogizawa one-way trip, so a full crossing should be treated as the day’s main job. The most useful summer plan gives Murodo the biggest flexible sightseeing block, treats Daikanbo and Kurobedaira as visibility-dependent stops, protects real walking time at Kurobe Dam, and forwards large luggage instead of carrying it through every transfer. The hidden decision is direction: start on the side where you sleep, finish on the side where the wider itinerary already needs to go, and do not cross the mountain merely to cross it. ↔ Scroll table left or right | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | **Your trip**
For another take on the same stay decision, compare [Tateyama Kurobe Autumn Leaves: Foliage Timing by Elevation from Murodo to the Dam](https://valunavi.com/post/tateyama-kurobe-autumn-leaves-timing-guide/). | **Best structure** | **Main reason** | | Toyama/Kanazawa → Nagano/Matsumoto | One-way west-to-east crossing | The Alpine Route replaces a transfer day instead of creating a separate out-and-back day | | Nagano/Matsumoto → Toyama/Kanazawa | One-way east-to-west crossing | Same logic in reverse; finish where the next hotel belongs | | Only Murodo matters | Return from Toyama side | A full crossing adds Dam/Ogizawa transport you may not value | | Only Kurobe Dam matters | Return from Ogizawa side | A full westward crossing is unnecessary if Murodo is not a priority | | Large suitcase | Use official same-day forwarding where your endpoints qualify | Repeated stairs, transfers and vehicle changes make large luggage a high-friction companion | | Late start | Cut sightseeing or switch to a shorter return trip | Intermediate sightseeing time competes directly with the final connections | ## Start with the route job: crossing or sightseeing return? The Alpine Route becomes much easier to justify when it performs two jobs at once: mountain sightseeing _and_ moving you from one region to another. If you sleep in Toyama, cross to Ogizawa and continue toward Nagano, the transport day has advanced the itinerary. Returning to Toyama after the full crossing would duplicate movement. The opposite is true when only one headline stop matters. If your goal is a summer walk at Murodo, a Toyama-side return can be cleaner. If your goal is Kurobe Dam and the trip already lives on the Nagano side, Ogizawa return access avoids paying with an entire day simply to reach Toyama. Use this deletion test: **if you removed Kurobe Dam from the day, would you still want to finish on the opposite side?** If yes, cross. If no, a return trip may be the more honest itinerary. ## A 7–8 hour “required time” is not seven hours of sightseeing The official 2026 same-day ticket page gives a Dentetsu Toyama → Ogizawa one-way required time of roughly 7–8 hours. That figure is useful because it destroys the idea that the Alpine Route is a quick attraction between breakfast and dinner plans. The day contains several different time costs: - getting from Toyama to Tateyama Station or from Nagano/Shinano-Omachi toward Ogizawa; - waiting for the reserved departure at the entry transport; - transferring between vehicles; - Murodo walking and food; - view stops at Daikanbo/Kurobedaira; - walking across Kurobe Dam; - the final bus/rail connection to the next hotel. A nine-hour sightseeing allowance therefore does not mean nine hours at the mountain stops. Every extra 30 minutes at an intermediate station is 30 minutes removed from the downstream connection margin. ## Murodo should receive the largest flexible block Murodo is the stop where the route becomes more than transport. At roughly 2,450 metres, it has plateau walks and alpine scenery close to the terminal. For a summer through-crossing, I would normally protect around 90 minutes to two hours here when conditions are good. That is not an official recommended duration. It is a planning allowance designed to let you walk, use the restroom, eat or drink, and still leave without treating the next vehicle as an emergency. If visibility is poor, the answer changes. Do not spend two hours waiting for a mountain view simply because a spreadsheet assigned two hours. Shorten the Murodo block and buy a larger connection margin farther along the route. Mountain weather makes flexibility more valuable than itinerary completion. ## Daikanbo and Kurobedaira are conditional stops, not mandatory long visits Daikanbo and Kurobedaira can deliver spectacular views when the weather cooperates. But on a cloudy day, extending both stops creates little marginal value while increasing queue and timing risk. I would use a visibility rule: - **Clear:** take the viewpoint time. - **Broken cloud:** allow a short look but keep moving if the next connection is good. - **Fully obscured:** treat them mainly as transfers and protect Murodo or Kurobe Dam instead. This keeps the route responsive to the actual mountain rather than to a list written months before the trip. ## Kurobe Dam needs walking time because the walk is part of the transfer Kurobe Dam is not a viewpoint beside a station where you step off, take one photograph and board the same train. The route physically carries you through the dam area between transport modes. Protect at least an hour around the dam if you want to walk the structure, use viewpoints and avoid turning the crossing into a race. If the group is tired or the route is running late, cut optional viewpoints before cutting the connection margin. This is especially important late in the day. The dam is visually impressive, but missing the final onward bus is a much larger itinerary cost than missing one upper observation point. ## Direction should follow the night before and the night after **West to east — Toyama/Tateyama → Ogizawa:** strongest when the previous night is Toyama or Kanazawa and the next night belongs in Nagano, Shinano-Omachi or Matsumoto. Murodo arrives earlier in the sightseeing sequence, which is useful when the plateau is the main attraction. **East to west — Ogizawa → Tateyama/Toyama:** strongest when the itinerary comes from Nagano or Matsumoto and continues to Toyama/Kanazawa. Kurobe Dam comes early, while Murodo becomes the larger alpine block later in the day. Do not reverse the route because one blog says a particular direction has “better views.” The larger value usually comes from deleting a hotel-transfer detour. Geography beats a minor sequencing preference. ## Reserve the entry time, then understand what is not reserved The official Alpine Route FAQ says the Tateyama Cable Car from Tateyama Station and the Kanden Tunnel Electric Bus from Ogizawa require designated boarding times. Official web tickets let you reserve that entry departure. Other intermediate stations do not work as one continuous reserved itinerary; you move through them according to the operating timetable and local boarding process. This creates a useful distinction: - **Entry reservation:** protects when you enter the mountain transport chain. - **Intermediate timing:** still depends on how long you stop, queues and the live timetable. A reserved 08:00 start is not a reservation for every ropeway and bus until 17:00. You still need to monitor progress through the day. ## If web tickets are sold out, the day is not automatically sold out The official FAQ states that same-day tickets can remain available even when web-ticket inventory is sold out, although the departure time you want may be unavailable and waiting may increase. That is useful for flexible travellers, but it should not be interpreted as a reason to avoid advance booking on a high-priority day. If the Alpine Route is the bridge between two prepaid hotels, an uncertain entry time has much higher cost than it does for someone staying two nights in Toyama. Use web tickets when the date and direction are already committed. Use same-day flexibility when weather could make you abandon the route without damaging the rest of the itinerary. ## Large luggage has an official same-day alternative The Alpine Route’s official 2026 baggage-forwarding service is one of the highest-value pieces of the route that many first-time visitors overlook. For the 2026 season, same-day forwarding operates from April 15 to November 8 on specified endpoint pairs. The current headline cross-route section is **Dentetsu Toyama Station / eligible Tateyama-side hotels ↔ Shinano Omachi Station / eligible Omachi Onsen hotels** at JPY 4,000 per item. Reception and collection windows vary by endpoint, and not every hotel or station pair is supported. The planning implication is more important than the price: **your suitcase can travel around the mountain while you travel through it.** That removes a large amount of stair, platform and vehicle friction. Do not assume the service connects directly to Nagano Station or every hotel. Check the official endpoint list and receiving deadline before building the day. If your wider trip needs normal hotel-to-hotel delivery instead, use the [Japan luggage-forwarding guide](https://valunavi.com/post/japan-luggage-forwarding-takkyubin-guide-1/) and send the main bag ahead one or more days earlier. ## Families, older travellers and strollers need a transfer count, not just a distance estimate The official FAQ notes that elevators are only available at limited points and recommends compact strollers because the route contains many stairs and transfers. Wheelchairs are available at stations for backup/emergency use, but one wheelchair cannot simply be used continuously through the entire route. That does not make the Alpine Route inaccessible to every family or older traveller. It changes the planning metric. Count: - how many vehicle changes the group can handle; - whether someone can manage stairs repeatedly; - whether the stroller folds quickly; - whether large luggage has been removed; - how much standing/waiting is acceptable. A slow group should shorten optional walking before it shortens transfer margin. ## Weather is the reason one sightseeing block must remain removable Summer at Murodo can be much cooler, wetter and windier than Toyama city. Pack an insulating layer and rain protection even when the lowland forecast looks comfortable. More importantly, make one block removable. For example: - Murodo walk = protected when visibility is good; - Daikanbo long viewpoint stop = removable; - Kurobedaira garden time = removable; - Kurobe Dam crossing = protected because it is part of the route; - final connection = never treated as removable. This creates a stop-loss rule. When the day falls 45 minutes behind, you already know what disappears first. ## A practical west-to-east summer crossing **Early morning:** leave Toyama with enough margin to collect any ticket and reach the reserved Tateyama-side departure. **Morning:** move through Bijodaira and the Highland Bus without adding unnecessary stops unless one is genuinely part of the plan. **Late morning / midday:** use the largest flexible block at Murodo. Walk only as far as the weather, group and timetable justify. **Early afternoon:** treat Daikanbo and Kurobedaira according to visibility. **Later afternoon:** protect Kurobe Dam time, then continue to Ogizawa. **Evening:** continue to the next hotel with a pre-checked bus/rail connection rather than deciding after reaching Ogizawa. The east-to-west version reverses the sequence but not the principle: one major alpine block, conditional viewpoints, one protected dam block and a final connection with real margin. ## When should you not do the full crossing? I would not use the full one-way route when: - the next hotel is back on the side where you started; - you only care about one end of the route; - the group cannot comfortably handle repeated transfers; - a late start leaves no margin at Murodo or the dam; - the weather is poor enough that the mountain day no longer justifies a long cross-region transfer. In those cases, a shorter return journey or a completely different day can have higher value. “I crossed the Alpine Route” is not itself a travel outcome worth protecting at any cost. ## Final verdict **The best summer Alpine Route is usually a one-way transfer day that advances the wider itinerary.** Cross west-to-east when Toyama/Kanazawa is behind you and Nagano/Matsumoto is next; reverse it when the trip is moving west. Give Murodo the biggest flexible block, keep Daikanbo and Kurobedaira conditional, and protect real time at Kurobe Dam. Reserve the entry departure when the route is a fixed bridge between hotels, remove large luggage with the official forwarding service when your endpoints qualify, and predefine what gets cut if the day slips. The route becomes stressful when every stop is treated as mandatory. It becomes elegant when sightseeing, transport and luggage all move in the same direction. - [Hakone Autumn Leaves Guide: Foliage Timing from Gora to Lake Ashi and Hakone-Yumoto](https://valunavi.com/post/hakone-autumn-guide/) - [Hokkaido Summer 5 Days: Sapporo & Otaru or Add Furano and Biei?](https://valunavi.com/post/hokkaido-summer-5-days-sapporo-otaru-or-furano-biei-1/) - [Naha Without a Car: A 2-Day Yui Rail, Shuri, Tsuboya and Kokusai Route](https://valunavi.com/post/naha-2-day-no-car-itinerary/) - [Mt. Takao Autumn Leaves Day Trip: Cable Car, Trails and Timing](https://valunavi.com/post/mt-takao-autumn-leaves/) - [Japan Autumn Leaves in September: Hokkaido, Alpine Routes and Grass Foliage](https://valunavi.com/post/japan-autumn-leaves-in-september/) ## References [Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route — 2026 date-specific timetables](https://tateyama-kurobe.com/en/timetable/) · [Official same-day ticket page — current fares and planning times](https://tateyama-kurobe.com/en/same-day-tickets/) · [Official FAQ — reserved entry transport, same-day tickets, facilities and accessibility](https://tateyama-kurobe.com/en/faq/) · [Official 2026 same-day baggage forwarding service](https://tateyama-kurobe.com/en/baggage/) · [Official announcements and live operational notices](https://tateyama-kurobe.com/en/announcement/). Checked August 25, 2026; the timetable changes by date, especially in November, so verify the exact travel day. # Climbing The Roof Of Japan – The Ultimate Guide To Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route

Last updated Feb 22, 2024

\|

[117 comments](https://nerdnomads.com/alpine-route-japan#comments)

![](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/avatar-privacy/cache/user/b/f/bf2a48db3dccb7f3383ad83a74464088a26a40bc25c15c75c7829f992d122358-100.jpg)

_Written by_

[Maria Wulff Hauglann](https://nerdnomads.com/about/)

Maria is the co-founder of Nerd Nomads. She's explored more than thirty countries and been a full time traveler since 2018.

Travel writer and co-founder of Nerd Nomads.

![The Ultimate Guide To Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route Japan](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Ultimate-Guide-To-Tateyama-Kurobe-Alpine-Route-Japan.jpg)

Dear Reader: We may get commissions for purchases made through links in this article, at no extra cost to you. This helps keep the site running and free for all. Thank you!❤️

_If you want to see the Japan Alps with stunning mountain views, beautiful green and lush valleys, the famous and impressive 18-m tall snow wall, and turquoise lakes, then the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route is a must! Read on to get everything you need to know about the Japan Alpine Route – how to get there, how to get tickets, how long it takes, and a description of the nine sections of the route._

After some days in the big, bustling [Tokyo City](https://nerdnomads.com/what-to-do-in-tokyo), we were ready to dig deeper into Japan and discover its more relaxed green side. So, a Swedish couple we met on a train in Kyoto said: “ _What do Norwegians do when they get to a country with mountains?!_”

Yep, you guessed it, since we come from a country full of mountains and fjords and therefore obviously love mountains, we headed inland to the Japan Alps to do the stunning **Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route**, also called **The Japanese Alpine Route**. It was one of the biggest highlights of our entire trip to Japan! 🙂 You can see our [Japan itinerary here](https://nerdnomads.com/japan-two-week-itinerary).

# Ultimate Guide To Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route

The Japan Alps is a fairly big area inland of mid-Japan, with a few big cities such as Nagano, Matsumoto, and Toyama. This area is a nature bliss packed with high mountains, rivers, lakes, forests, and wilderness. It surely is a hiker\`s delight!

We decided to travel/ hike along the spectacular Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route when we visited Japan, and we loved it! It was so refreshing after spending weeks in the big cities of [Singapore](https://nerdnomads.com/singapore-itinerary), [Bangkok](https://nerdnomads.com/what-to-do-in-bangkok), [Kuala Lumpur](https://nerdnomads.com/best-things-kuala-lumpur), and [Tokyo](https://nerdnomads.com/what-to-do-in-tokyo)!

In this guide.

* * *

## What Is Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route?

Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route is a popular and scenic 90 km route that crosses the northern part of the Japanese Alps from the east (Shinano Omachi Station) to the west (Toyama Station). You take different means of transport to get over the mountain pass, like cable cars and switch-back trains. You decide for yourself how much walking you want to do.

These Northern Alps, also called the Hida Mountains, stretch through Nagano, Toyama, and Gifu prefectures with several tall mountain peaks. The tallest mountain along the Japan Alpine Route is Mt. Tateyama (3015 m).

**The Alpine Route is open from the 15th of April to the 30th of November.**

The Alpine Route is completely closed during winter, from the 1st of December until the 14th of April.

The Alpine Route connects **Shinano Omachi Station** on the east side of the Japan Alps with **Toyama Station** on the west side (see the map below), and takes about 6-7 hours in total:

_Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route goes from east to west through the northern part of the Japanese Alps. You will take eight different means of transport. The whole trip takes 6-7 hours (although we used 9 as we did some hiking too)._

It is an incredible journey through sacred mountains, wilderness, forests, impressive tunnels, high peaks, hot springs, and Japan\`s highest dam, Kurobe Dam. Plus, a ton of fresh mountain air!

### Snow Wall

In spring, April – June, the Alpine Route is literally carved through the snow, making an impressive 18-meter-high snow wall! The **snow wall** is a huge attraction in Japan and is a fantastic sight! Even at the end of June, the snow wall is usually over 10 meters high.

### Autumn Colors

In autumn, September – November, the leaves change color from green to beautiful **autumn colors** of red, yellow, orange, and brown. It is a stunning sight!

## Alpine Route From East To West

We did the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route from east to west, starting in **Shinano Omachi** and ending up in **Toyama**.

You can do the Alpine Route in either direction, also from west to east (Toyama to Shinano Omachi). Most people do it one way only, but you can do it as a round-trip. Or you can only do half the Alpine Route and make a return trip to Murodo, which is the route´s highest point.

This guide describes how to do the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route from east to west, starting in Matsumoto and ending in Toyama, and on to Kanazawa.

The Alpine Route is divided into nine stops and eight sections, each with different means of transport and walking distances.

[![A map of the Japan Alpine Route](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20389'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Japan-Alpine-Route.png) The Japan Alpine Route goes from Shinano Omachi (east) to Toyama (west).

### The Alpine Route's 9 Stops

The Alpine Route has 9 stops and 8 sections of different means of transport (from east to west):

1. **Shinano Omachi**


Section 1: Bus from Shinano Omachi to Ogizawa (40 min)
2. **Ogizawa**


Section 2: Trolley Bus from Ogizawa to Kurobe Dam (16 min)
3. **Kurobe Dam**


Section 3: Cable Car from Kurobe Dam to Kurobedaira (5 min)
4. **Kurobedaira**


Section 4: Tateyama Ropeway from Kurobedaira to Daikanbo (7 min)
5. **Daikanbo**


Section 5: Trolley Bus from Daikanbo to Murodo (10 min)
6. **Murodo** – _Alpine Route's highest point, 2450 m above sea level_


Section 6: Bus from Murodo to Bijodaira (50 min)
7. **Bijodaira**


Section 7: Cable Car from Bijodaira to Tateyama (7 min)
8. **Tateyama**


Section 8: Train from Tateyama Station to Toyama Station (1 hour)
9. **Toyama**

A great place to spend the night before doing the Alpine Route is [Matsumoto](https://nerdnomads.com/matsumoto) (like we did, as it is only a 1-hour train ride from Shinano Omachi) or Nagano (a 2,5-hour train ride from Shinano Omachi). And from Toyama, I recommend you go to [Kanazawa](https://nerdnomads.com/kanazawa) (a 35-minute train ride from Toyama) to spend a few nights.

Getting To The Start of Alpine Route (Shinano Omachi):

### Tokyo – Matsumoto – Shinano Omachi

From [Tokyo](https://nerdnomads.com/what-to-do-in-tokyo), we took the train to [Matsumoto City](https://nerdnomads.com/matsumoto) (a 4-hour train trip), where we stayed the night at the hotel [Onyado Nono Matsumoto Natural Hot Spring](https://nerdnomads.com/go/onyado-nono-hotel-matsumoto) (the only decent hotel in Matsumoto, in our opinion).

Early the next morning, we took the train **from Matsumoto Station to Shinano Omachi Station** – the start of the Alpine Route (a 1-hour train trip).

You can also start from, for instance, **Nagano**. The train trip from Nagano to Shinano Omachi takes about 2,5 hours.

We bought [the Japan Railway Pass (JR Pass) online](https://nerdnomads.com/go/jr_rail_pass) before entering Japan, which we used on these two train trips (Tokyo – Matsumoto and Matsumoto – Shinano Omachi).

#### Matsumoto

Matsumoto is a relatively small valley city by Japanese standards (243,000 inhabitants) embraced by seven tall peaks (all above 3000 m) and three smaller ones. The valley where Matsumoto is situated is no more than 20 km across at its widest. It is a cozy little city with one of Japan's biggest attractions – **Matsumoto Castle**, or Crow Castle, as it is also called due to its black and white color.

We stayed at [Onyado Nono Matsumoto Natural Hot Spring](https://nerdnomads.com/go/onyado-nono-hotel-matsumoto). This is the only decent hotel in Matsumoto, to be honest.

We woke up at the crack of dawn in Matsumoto, checked out of the hotel, and took the 08:00 (8 am) train to Shinano-Omachi Station, where the Alpine Route starts.

⇒ **Read Next:  [Our Ultimate Guide to Matsumoto](https://nerdnomads.com/matsumoto)**

Stop 1 – 721 m above sea level:

### Shinano Omachi

Shinano Omachi is where the Alpine Route starts on the eastern side.

When we arrived at the Shinano-Omachi Station, we went straight over to the **Baggage Forwarding Service** office to drop off our backpacks.

#### Baggage Forwarding Service

The Baggage Forwarding Service office (marked “ _Alps Roman Kan_“) is on your right when you get out of the Shinano Omachi Train Station.

The cost per bag is **2500 JPY from Shinano Omachi Station to Toyama Station** (where the Alpine Route ends on the west side). It might feel a little expensive, but it is really a must-do, as traveling with big bags and suitcases on the Alpine Route would be really uncomfortable.

The Alpine Route Forwarding Service Office at Shinano Omachi Station is open from 07:40 to 10:30 for drop-off.

You can then pick up your bags at the end of the Alpine Route (the west side) – **Toyama Station** (between 15:30 and 18:00). The baggage forwarding service was, however, not open for service in November 2023 (the last day was 31. October 2023). So, if you are doing the Alpine Route in November, you should check if the baggage forwarding service is still operative.

You can also have your bags picked up at your hotel and delivered to your next hotel. [Read more about the Baggage Forwarding Service here](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/transport/baggage.html).

[![DSC01112](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01112.jpg) The Alpine Route Baggage Office

After we got rid of our bags, we jumped on the bus to Stop 2 of the Alpine Route: **Ogizawa** (the bus departs right in front of the Shinano-Omachi Station).

[![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01113.jpg)

Bus ticket office.

[![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01116.jpg)

On the bus to from Shinano-Omachi Ogizawa.

_Section 1: Take the bus from Shinano-Omachi to Ogizawa (a 40-minute bus ride)._

Stop 2 – 1433 m asl:

### Ogizawa

The bus ride from **Shinano-Omachi to Ogizawa** takes about 40 minutes.

During that time, the weather, unfortunately, turned really bad! It was raining cats and dogs! 🙁 Ah, how unlucky! Our mood sank, and we started to think that we had not picked the right day for our Alpine Route adventure and regretted the whole thing.

[![DSC01133](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01133.jpg) View from the bus ride to Ogizawa. It was raining a LOT! 🙁[![DSC01124](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01124.jpg) Ogizawa trolley-bus station. The weather situation was not looking good…..

When we arrived at **Ogizawa**, it was raining heavily. We even thought about skipping the Alpine Route and returning to Tokyo. But we had already handed in our luggage at Shinano-Omachi Station for baggage forwarding to Toyama Station, so there was no turning back.

[![DSC01121](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01121.jpg) Buying tickets for the Alpine Route.

We made the 10:00 trolley bus departure from Stop 2: Ogizawa to Stop 3: **Kurobe Dam**.

The trolley bus ride was pretty cool and took us through a 5,8 km tunnel up to the giant Kurobe Dam. The trolley bus ride took 16 minutes.

[![DSC01139](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01139.jpg) Lots of people on the 10:00 AM trolley bus through the 5,8 km long tunnel. Mostly Japanese tourists.

_Section 2: Take the trolley bus from Ogizawa to Kurobe Dam (a 16-minute ride)._

Stop 3 – 1470 m asl :

### Kurobe Dam

When we exited the trolley bus and the tunnel, the weather had improved and stopped raining! Yay! We were so happy! 🙂

The Kurobe Dam is Japan\`s highest dam (186 m) and a very impressive sight!

[![Kurobe Dam Japan](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20441'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC8520.jpg) The Kurobe Dam, Japan's highest

### Kurobe Dam Observation Deck

We climbed the 220 steps up to the Observation Desk from the trolley bus station.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20468%20705'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin

Lots of steps up to the Observation Deck.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20468%20705'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20468%20705'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin

Great view from the stairs.

Once on top, we were rewarded with amazing views over the dam and its surroundings! All the steps were totally worth it! 🙂

[![DSC01219](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01219.jpg) The Kurobe Dam[![Japanese Mountains](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20468'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC8572.jpg) Beautiful mountain views from the Kurobe Dam

Incredibly, 10 tons of water shoot out of the dam every second! EVERY SECOND! Oh my god, that is a LOT of water! 🙂

[![DSC01151](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01151.jpg) 10 tons of water pours out from the dam every second!

After World War II, Japan had a sudden economic boom and faced a severe energy shortage. To generate additional electricity, the government invested in hydroelectric power and decided to build the Kurobe Dam.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin

Impressive and a bit scary to stand on the dam and look down on the water.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20471%20705'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin

The water pours down into a beautiful valley with a river.

Unbelievably, 10 million people worked on the dam during its construction! The hardest part was apparently digging the tunnel that the Kanden Tunnel Trolleybus now runs through.

After the dam's construction, a movie entitled “ _Sun over Kurobe_” was released starring famous Japanese actors. This film gave the Kurobe Dam a legendary status similar to the Hoover Dam in the USA.

[![_DSC8487](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20468'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC8487.jpg) When standing on the deck close to the dam, one could really feel and hear the water pressure.[![Kurobe Dam](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01155.jpg) You can walk across the Kurobe Dam on a walkway.

### Kurobe Dam Museum

Inside the mountain is a museum where you can read and see a movie from when the dam was built.

Unfortunately, not much of it is in English. Here is also a memorial monument to the 171 workers who sadly lost their lives during the construction of the dam.

[![History of Kurobe Dam](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20705%20471'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Pin](https://nerdnomads.com/wp-content/uploads/DSC01208.jpg) A small museum at the Kurobe Dam tells the story of how it was built

## Summary: Alpine Route Step-By-Step

Altogether, we spent approximately 9 hours on the entire Alpine Route:

1\. **Train [Matsumoto](https://nerdnomads.com/matsumoto) – Shinano Omachi**  (1 hour)

This train is NOT included in the Alpine Route ticket, so you have to buy this train ticket separately.

We bought a 14-day [Japan Rail Pass](https://nerdnomads.com/go/jr_rail_pass), which we used on this train ride. However, this pass is only for tourists, and you have to buy it outside of Japan before you go there. You can order a JR Pass online from official JR Pass agents such as [JRailPass.com](https://nerdnomads.com/go/jr_rail_pass).

[Click here for prices & information on how to order the JR Pass online](https://nerdnomads.com/go/jr_rail_pass)

Shinano-Omachi Train Station is where the baggage forwarding service is (open for drop-off from 07:40 to 10:30). Hand in your luggage here, and it will be delivered to the other end of the Alpine Route – Toyama Station (must be picked up before 18:00).

2\. **Bus Shinano-Omachi – Ogizawa**  (40 min)

3\. **Trolleybus Ogizawa – Kurobe Dam**  (16 min)

At Kurobe Dam, we spent some time, maybe about 1,5 hours. We walked around, took pictures, and had a look at the small museum. You can spend less time there or more time. There is also a small ferry cruise on the dam (takes 2,5 hours), but we did not take this.

4\. **Cable Car Kurobe Dam – Kurobedaira**  (5 min)

We did not spend much time at Kurobedaira. We had lunch at a cafe (maybe 30 minutes).

5\. **Ropeway Kurobedaira – Daikanbo** (7 min)

We did not spend much time at Daikanbo. It is not a big area to walk on; it is just a platform/viewpoint.

6\. **Trolleybus Daikanbo – Murodo** (10 min)

This is the highest point of the Alpine Route. Now you are really in the mountains and can go for long or short walks. We spent maybe 1,5 hours here altogether. We hiked the Mukurigaike Pond Loop (1 hour). But we did not take a bath in the Onsen at Mukurigaike Inn (which I regret).

From Murodo, you can also climb Mt. Tateyama (it takes about 4 hours).

7\. **Bus Murodo – Bijodaira** (50 min)

We spent basically no time in Bijodaira, only waiting for the cable car. But you can do walks from Bijodaira too, or jump off the bus on its way from Murodo to Bijodaira to do walks along the way. We did not do this.

8\. **Cable Car Bijodaira – Tateyama** (7 min)

We spent no time in Tateyama, only waiting for the train. You can choose to end your Alpine Route journey here if you want to sleep in Tateyama. But there is not much to see in Tateyama.

9\. **Train Tateyama – Toyama** (1 hour)

Toyama is the end of the Alpine Route and the end of the Alpine Route ticket. Here, we picked up our bags (we picked them up around 17:00, the Baggage Forwarding Office closes at 18:00).

10\. **Train Toyama – Kanazawa** (35 min)

We chose to go to Kanazawa immediately, and not sleep in Toyama as we had heard that Kanazawa is a nicer city with much more to see. But you can, of course, sleep in Toyama. It is quite a big city. We reached Kanazawa around 18:00/ 6 pm.

If you want to do the same, and spend a few days in Kanazawa, [check out our ultimate guide to Kanazawa](https://nerdnomads.com/kanazawa) and our [recommended places to stay in Kanazawa](https://nerdnomads.com/where-to-stay-in-kanazawa). Kanazawa quickly became our favorite city in Japan and is a must-visit in our opinion.

## How To Buy Tickets

The only place you can reserve tickets for the Alpine Route is [here (the official website of Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route)](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/).

The ticket is valid for five days after you have exchanged your WEB reservation ticket for an actual ticket at the ticket office (for instance, at Ogizawa Station if you start on the east side or at Tateyama Station if you start on the west side of the route).

You can, of course, buy Alpine Route tickets directly at the Ogizawa Station or Tateyama Station (depending on which side you want to start the Alpine Route) without any reservations. But I recommend that you make a ticket reservation if you plan on doing the Alpine Route during the peak seasons of spring (April, May & June) and autumn (September & October).

We did the Alpine Route in July and had no problems getting tickets without any reservations. We just showed up at Ogizawa Station (we came from Matsumoto Station to Ogizawa Station) in the morning and bought the ticket at the ticket counter for the same day.

## How Much Does It Cost?

The Alpine Route ticket for the full route one-way (East: Shinano Omachi to West: Dentetsu Toyama, or the other way around) costs:

- 13820 Yen for adult
- 6930 Yen for child (6-11 years old)
- Children below six years old can do the Alpine Route for free

The Alpine Route is unfortunately **not covered by the JR Pass**.

But you can use the JR Pass to get to the start of the Alpine Route. You can use the JR Pass to get to Shinano Omachi Station if you want to start on the east side of the Alpine Route or to Dentetsu Toyama Station if you want to start on the west side.

We used JR Passes to get from Tokyo (via one night in Matsumoto) to Shinano Omachi Station, where we started our Alpine Route trip.

[See the fares for the Alpine Route tickets here](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/transport/fare.html)

## Doing The Alpine Route Over 2-3 Days

We did the Alpine Route as a day trip (between Matsumoto and Kanazawa), but doing it over 2-3 days is a great idea. Then you can do more hiking and see more of the stunning mountain landscape. It is also a bit more relaxed, and you can enjoy it more.

The best place to stay when doing the Alpine Route over several days is to stay at one of the hotels along the route or at either of the starting points – Shinano-Omachi Station (east side of the route) or Toyama (west side).

### Hotels Along The Alpine Route

[Hotel Tateyama](https://nerdnomads.com/go/hotel_tateyama_japan)

Hotel Tateyama is a resort hotel located at the highest point of the Alpine Route – Murodo (see step 6. Murodo in this article), 2 450 meters above sea level. The hotel is at the center of the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route. The panoramic view of the 3,000-meter mountains surrounding the hotel is stunning! It is an excellent place to go hiking.

The hotel has several free tours like a bus tour to see the sunrise from a mountain top, a snow wall walking tour, a star gazing tour, and a bird-watching tour. You also get to borrow snow boots and trekking poles for free. This is the best place to stay if you want to hike Mt. Tateyama.

The hotel offers a baggage forwarding service (to and from the hotel) and free lockers where you can leave your belongings after check-out and explore the area. The hotel's hot spring (onsen) is fantastic; you can even book a private bath. The set dinner is excellent, too, with high-quality food (Japanese and French). The WIFI is quite strong. ## When To Go?

The closing and opening dates for the Alpine Route Tateyama Kurobe are (every year):

- **Open: 15. April  – 30. November**
- **Closed: 1. December – 14. April**

The Alpine Route is awesome all year round (when it is open), and each season has its highlight:

### Spring – April, May & June

When the route opens in mid-April, you can see huge and impressive 18-meter-tall snow/ice walls on each side of the road. This melts during April, May, and June and is more or less completely gone in July.

In June, spring is on in the mountains with beautiful spring flowers, birds singing, and everything gets green. Even in late June, the snow walls are still over 10 meters high. There will be fewer visitors in June so that you can enjoy a more relaxing experience.

### Summer – July & August

Summer is the best season for hiking, sightseeing, climbing, and walking in the mountains, as the temperatures are pleasantly warm. There is still some snow at the route's highest point (Murodo) that you can play around with.

### Autumn – September, October & November

The autumn is in September/ October, turning nature into stunning colors of yellow, orange, and red. The leaves take six weeks to change color, and it begins at the end of September.

The autumn colors last until the beginning of November. The change begins in higher areas and moves down the mountain. You can see all kinds of colors and white snow-covered mountain peaks during a trip. Stunning!

* * *

## How Long Does It Take?

The Tatekyama Kurobe Alpine Route takes **at least six to seven hours**, depending on the wait for transport and how much hiking you want to do.

We used nine hours all together from Matsumoto to Kanazawa:

- Transport: 4,5 hours from Matsumoto to Toyama. 35 min more to [Kanazawa](https://nerdnomads.com/kanazawa).
- Walking and waiting for transport: 4,5 hours (can be done faster or longer)
- **Total time spent on the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route: 9 hours**

We spent the exact same amount of time on transport and on walking/ waiting for transport.

* * *

## How To Get To The Alpine Route?

### Train

You can do the Alpine Route from east to west or west to east.

From east to west: Take the train to **Shinano Omachi Station** from either Nagano Station (a 1 2,5 hour train ride) or Matsumoto Station (a 1-hour train ride).

From west to east: Take the train to **Toyama Station**.

* * *

## Baggage Delivery Service

We dropped off our luggage at the Baggage Forwarding Service counter at the Shinano-Omachi Station, also called “Alps Roman Kan” (located just next to JR Shinano Omachi Station).

Drop-off time is between 07:40 and 10:30 am; no reservation is needed. You are given a baggage forwarding tag that you fill out and attach to your luggage, and it will be delivered to the Alpine Route's end stop – Toyama Station.

Your bags can be reclaimed at Toyama train station between 15:30 (3:30 pm) and 18:00 (6 pm). The cost per bag is 2500 JPY from Shinano Omachi Station to Toyama Station.

You can also have your luggage shipped directly from your hotel to the next hotel you plan to stay at. [Read more about that here](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/transport/baggage.html).

Obs! In 2023, the forwarding service ended on 31. October. So, if you plan on doing the Alpine Route in November, you should check if the baggage forwarding service is still operative.

* * *

It is possible only to do parts of this trip and also do it the other way around. You can get more information about this trip on the Alpine Route webpage: [http://www.alpen-route.com/en/](http://www.alpen-route.com/en/)

⇒We love the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, and it is on our recommended [two-week Japan Itinerary, which you can find here](https://nerdnomads.com/japan-two-week-itinerary)

Unfortunately, you cannot see Mount Fuji on this alpine route. If seeing Mt Fuji is on your bucket list, you should consider visiting [Hakone](https://nerdnomads.com/hakone-travel-itinerary) and/ or [Fuji Five Lakes](https://nerdnomads.com/mt-fuji-five-lakes-kawaguchiko), which are close to Tokyo (1,5 – 2 hours train ride).

      The Baggage Forwarding Service where you hand in your bags by yourself at the baggage forwarding service center at Shinano-Omachi Station (we did this) is only open until the 10th of November.       The Baggage Forwarding Service where they pick up bags at hotels in Tateyama and Midagahara, plus from Toyama Station to Nagano Station is only available until the 4th of November.



      This is what is written at the official website of the Alpine Route:



      Service available: April 15th – November 10th.


      Hotel Tateyama & Midagahara Hotel: April 29th – November 4th.


      Dentetsu Toyama－Nagano Station: April 15th – November 4th.(4/15-11/4)



      **Where To Book Alpine Route Tickets Online**



      The only place you can reserve Alpine Route tickets is at [the official Alpine Route Webpage](https://tateyama-kurobe.alpen-route.com/en/). But there are several tour agents that arrange tours where the Alpine Route is included (see a list further down).



      I see that for November 2019 (the last square at the bottom of [this page](https://tateyama-kurobe.alpen-route.com/en/) labeled “2019/ 11”) almost all dates are yellow. This means that you can only reserve tickets from Ogizawa and board the Alpine Route in Ogizawa on the east side of the Alpine Route. So you can only do the Alpine Route from the east (starting in Ogizawa) to the west (ending in Tateyama). And not the other way around, from Tateyama (west) to Ogizawa (east).



      We did the Alpine Route from east to west (from Ogizawa to Tateyama) and it was great!



      I see that there are lots of tickets available for the 6th of November, the date you want to do the Alpine Route, all departing times on this date are available.



      So you must get to Shinano-Omachi Station (for instance by train from Tokyo to Matsumoto, and then from Matsumoto to Shinano-Omachi). At Shinano-Omachi Station you drop off your bags at the Baggage Forwarding Service Office and buy a bus ticket to Ogizawa (which is not included in the Alpine Route Ticket). This bus ride takes about 40 min.



      In Ogizawa the Alpine Route starts. Here you exchange your web ticket reservation into an actual ticket at the ticket office. Or you can buy the tickets there directly (we bought ours there and did not make a web reservation).



      So you must do the Alpine Route from East to West:


      Shinano-Omachi Station (hand in your bags) – Ogizawa (the official start of the Alpine Route) – Tateyama (the official end of the Alpine Route) – Toyama (pick up your bags)

50. hi Maria.. i just read that ‘A partial route is open from the 10th to the 14th of April (between Dentetsu Toyama and Midagahara)’ .. is it possible for me to go there around 12 or 13 april? and what can we do there at that moment? thank you

    [Reply](https://nerdnomads.com/alpine-route-japan#comment-103644)

    - Hi Indriasari!



      The Alpine Route is closed from December 1st to April 14th. So the first day you can do the Alpine Route is on the **15\. April**.



      Unfortunately, it looks like there was no partial route open this year from 10. – 14. April 2023. Unless the partial route opens up again next year (2024), it looks like the first day you can go is on the 15. April. So it looks like you can not go there on the 12. or 13. April. Sorry about that.



      You should check the [official webpage of the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/) to see the opening date for 2024.



      The big thing on the Alpine Route in the spring (April – June), is the huge 18 m tall snow wall. The Alpine Route is literally carved through the snow in April, so the sight is quite impressive. You can read more about it here: [https://www.alpen-route.com/en/seasonal-attraction/spring.html](https://www.alpen-route.com/en/seasonal-attraction/spring.html)



      All the best,


      Maria

      [Reply](https://nerdnomads.com/alpine-route-japan#comment-103720)
51. Has alpine route got strictly fixed dates of opening?



    Our Family of 4 will be having nights of 7,8,9 April to spend between Kyoto to Tokyo.Just wondering if we should simply do Kanazawa day , Shirakawago night followed by Takayama day , Matsumoto night and then Shibuonsen night?



    Very confused

    [Reply](https://nerdnomads.com/alpine-route-japan#comment-107573)

    - Hi Jyoti!



      Yes, the Alpine Route has fixed opening days, the same dates every year. It is open from the **15th of April to the 30th of November**. So it is not open on your dates (7. – 9. April).



      With only three nights (7. – 9. April) to spend between Kyoto and Tokyo, it is way too ambitious to do Kanazawa, Shirakawago, Takayama, Matsumoto, and Shibu Onsen. You will not have time to see anything at each place. It is simply not doable, either, as it will take time to get between these places too. Do you plan on renting a car? This will, however, save you some traveling time.



      I suggests that you do either Kanazawa and/ or Takayama (with a day trip to Shirakawago). So for instance two nights in Kanazawa, then do Shirakawago on your way to Takayama. And one night in Takayama:



      – 6\. April: Take the train Kyoto – Kanazawa (a 2-hour train ride)


      – 6\. – 8. April (2 nights): Kanazawa


      – 8\. April: Take the bus Kanazawa – Takayama, with a stop in Shirakawago (a 2-hour bus ride Kanazawa – Takayama)


      – 8\. – 9. April (1 night): Takayama


      – 9\. April: Take the train Takayama – Tokyo (a 4-hour train ride)



      Have a fantastic trip to Japan in April!



      All the best,


      Maria

      [Reply](https://nerdnomads.com/alpine-route-japan#comment-107709)

      - Thanks a lot Maria.



        I was feeling suffocated with speed of my own plans 🙂 thanks helping me slow down.



        I read on websites that Kyoto and Kanazawa a pretty similar and Takayama gives more different feel . To add diversity to my trip ( but not on cost of missing places wort going in time I have ), do you think it will be good idea to skip kanazawa and rather do


        Kyoto to


        Takayama ( 1 night)


        +Shirakawago



        AND



        Matsumato ( 1 night)


        \+ Jigukundani (shibu onsen) ( 1 night)


        then to Tokyo



        I am really looking for suggestions and thanks again for your reply



        Jyoti 🙂

        [Reply](https://nerdnomads.com/alpine-route-japan#comment-107717)

        - Yes, you can skip Kanazawa, and do Matsumoto and Jigukundani instead.



          1 night in Matsumoto is enough (the biggest attraction there is Matsumoto Castle). But 1 night in Takayama might be stressful, especially if you want to do a day-trip to Shirakawago. The bus trip between Takayama and Shirakawago takes about 1 hour one way. But you might be able to do Shirakawago as a morning trip (leave your bags at Takayama Station and pick it up again before heading on to Matsumoto).



          The train trip Kyoto – Takayama is a bit longer than to Kanazawa. It is a 3,5 hour train trip, since the fast Shinkansen train does not go all the way to Takayama. You must take the Shinkansen to Nagoya Station, then change there to a rapid train up to Takayama.



          To get from Takamaya to Matsumoto, it is quickest to take the bus (2 h 40 min). The train trip takes 5-6 hours (via Toyama Station).



          So your itinerary will be something like this:



          – 6\. april: In the morning, take the train Kyoto – Takayama (3,5 hours)


          – 6\. – 7. april (1 night): Explore Takayama


          – 7\. april: Morning return bus ride Takayama – Shirakawago (2 hours return bus ride). In the afternoon/ evening, take the bus Takayama – Matsumoto (2,5 h bus ride). Stay 1 night in Matsumoto


          – 8\. april: Explore Matsumoto. In the afternoon, take the train/ bus to Shibu Onsen (2,5 h train ride Matsumoto Station – Yudanaka Station, then a 7-min taxiride to Shibu Onsen).



          I have added this itinerary to a [Google Maps which you can see here](https://maps.app.goo.gl/4XMjf8rxSuv6MAHo8).



          Have a great time in Japan!



          -Maria-
